name: Electric toothbrush

lead: An electric or powered toothbrush uses a motor to drive the brush head in oscillating-rotating, sonic or other high-frequency motions. Many models add pressure sensors and timers to guide a two-minute brushing routine.
For appearance, the practical gains are cleaner teeth, less stain-trapping plaque and healthier gums, which together support a brighter, fresher-looking smile.

paras: The motorized head performs thousands of strokes per minute, which removes plaque more consistently than most people manage by hand, and built-in timers and pressure alerts improve technique. Sonic models also create fluid movement around the bristles.

Side effects are rare and minor, mainly gum abrasion if pressed too hard. The large Cochrane review found modest but real advantages for powered brushes in plaque (about 11 to 21 percent) and gingivitis (about 6 to 11 percent), with the authors noting the clinical importance is uncertain. Premium marketing claims often exceed that evidence, so a mid-priced oscillating model is sufficient.
